_note: Course-layer codebook (D49): built inductively from 1,478 open-coding labels of 1,765 syllabus statements; content-only names, stance carried by the statement's stance tag. Not derived from the institutional types.

themes.label: AI and the code students submit

types.name: Default stance: AI not allowed
types.covers: AI is banned for the course or for all graded work ("no AI on graded work", "generative AI strictly prohibited").

types.name: Default stance: AI allowed or encouraged
types.covers: AI is allowed, welcomed or encouraged for course work ("AI use encouraged", "LLMs allowed on programming assignments", "AI assumed on projects").

types.name: Default stance: AI discouraged but allowed
types.covers: AI is permitted but students are advised against it ("AI allowed but not advisable", "asked to avoid AI on homework").

types.name: Rules vary by assignment or deliverable
types.covers: The AI rule is set per assignment, deliverable or activity, or the instructor may permit or ban AI case by case ("AI only on designated assignments", "per-assignment AI permission stated").

types.name: Fallback when an assignment is silent
types.covers: What applies when an assignment does not state an AI rule ("silence means AI not allowed", "ask if assignment silent").

types.name: Ask staff when unsure
types.covers: Students should ask the instructor or TAs when unsure whether an AI use is allowed.

types.name: Named levels of AI use
types.covers: The course uses levels or tiers of AI use (department levels, student-chosen levels, a level per milestone).

types.name: AI for understanding concepts and material
types.covers: AI as a tutor or explainer for concepts, syntax, language features and course material.

types.name: AI for debugging and error messages
types.covers: AI to interpret error messages, find bugs or explain failing tests (allowed, limited or banned).

types.name: AI feedback on one's own code or work
types.covers: AI reviews or critiques code, proofs or drafts the student wrote.

types.name: AI for tests and test cases
types.covers: AI to design, generate or brainstorm test cases (allowed, limited or banned).

types.name: AI for documentation, comments and formatting
types.covers: AI for docstrings, comments, type hints, formatting, boilerplate or editing non-code documents.

types.name: AI for study and practice
types.covers: AI for practice problems, mock quizzes, study questions and exam preparation.

types.name: AI for brainstorming and planning
types.covers: AI for ideas, breaking down an assignment, or planning an approach or design.

types.name: AI for search and reference
types.covers: AI used like a search engine or reference to look up information.

types.name: Course-provided AI tutor
types.covers: The course provides or prescribes its own AI tool or tutor prompt, often designed to guide without solving.

types.name: AI writing submitted code or solutions
types.covers: Whether AI may produce the code, answers or solutions students submit (most often banned).

types.name: Limits on how much AI code
types.covers: Caps or conditions on AI code: a few lines, snippets or examples only, no verbatim copying, rewrite it yourself.

types.name: Ask AI for explanations, not code
types.covers: Students may prompt AI for how-to explanations or hints but not for solution code; examples of appropriate and inappropriate prompts.

types.name: AI in the editor (autocomplete, Copilot, IDE assistants)
types.covers: Rules on AI built into editors and IDEs: disable code completion, Copilot or AI extensions, or allow them.

types.name: Agentic coding tools
types.covers: Rules on coding agents that act in the codebase (banned, allowed for experienced students, or the course is built around them).

types.name: Entering assignments, course materials or own code into AI
types.covers: Do not paste assignment text, course materials, lab code or one's own code into AI tools.

types.name: AI-written prose deliverables
types.covers: AI writing essays, reports, reflections, analyses or other written deliverables.

types.name: Own attempt first, then AI
types.covers: Try the problem or write and debug code yourself before turning to AI.

types.name: Disclosing AI use
types.covers: Students must disclose or acknowledge AI use (a statement, a note, a checkbox), including when none was used.

types.name: Citing AI in code
types.covers: Mark AI-derived code in comments, per line, function or file header.

types.name: Prompts, transcripts and logs
types.covers: Keep or submit prompts, full chat transcripts or session logs (prompts file, unedited transcripts, committed to the repository).

types.name: Reflection on AI use
types.covers: Reflect on how AI was used and what was learned (forms, paragraphs, retrospectives).

types.name: Disclosure safe harbor and nondisclosure
types.covers: Disclosed use is not penalized, and undisclosed or uncited use is the violation.

types.name: Understand and explain every line
types.covers: Students must understand and be able to explain any submitted code, sometimes orally or in a code review, with penalties if they cannot.

types.name: Verify and test AI output
types.covers: Students check AI output for correctness and are responsible for its errors.

types.name: Work must be one's own
types.covers: Submitted work must be the student's own, original work.

types.name: AI under collaboration rules
types.covers: AI is treated like a classmate, friend, outside helper or source under the course's collaboration and citation rules.

types.name: No AI during exams and quizzes
types.covers: AI is not allowed during exams, quizzes or in-class assessments.

types.name: Assessment designed around AI
types.covers: Proctored or paper quizzes and exams weighted more, screen recording, random code interviews, projects designed for minimal AI.

types.name: AI misuse as misconduct
types.covers: Unauthorized AI use counts as cheating, plagiarism or an honor-code violation.

types.name: Penalties for AI misuse
types.covers: Stated consequences: zero, grade reduction, course failure, report.

types.name: Detecting AI use
types.covers: Staff can detect AI work; similarity checks include AI-generated solutions; detectors used or explicitly not used.

types.name: Reporting and referral
types.covers: Suspected violations are reported to an honor council, dean or conduct office, or discussed with the student first.

types.name: AI undermines learning
types.covers: Using AI to do the work skips the practice that builds skill and understanding.

types.name: Fundamentals before AI
types.covers: Novices must learn the basics before relying on AI.

types.name: AI output is unreliable or insecure
types.covers: Warnings that AI code or answers can be wrong, insecure, outdated, poorly styled or ignore course constraints.

types.name: AI homework hurts exam performance
types.covers: Relying on AI for homework leaves students unprepared for unaided quizzes and exams.

types.name: Careers and industry
types.covers: Employers test unaided skills, or industry expects AI fluency: careers given as a reason either way.

types.name: Benefits of AI for learning
types.covers: AI is described as valuable for learning or as a skill worth building.

types.name: Ethics, privacy and cost
types.covers: Personal data in prompts, training-data consent, licensing, environmental cost, paid tools.

types.name: Opt-out and equal access
types.covers: Students may opt out of AI, can earn full marks without it, or need not buy a tool; accommodations.

types.name: Pointer to other policies
types.covers: Refers to the university, department or other courses' AI policies, which still apply.

types.name: AI as course content
types.covers: The course teaches AI tools or AI-assisted software engineering as a subject.

types.name: Sharing AI outputs, prompts or sessions
types.covers: Do not share prompts, outputs, transcripts or AI access with others.
